clue.text: Dress rehearsal for this ? On the contrary

definitions.text: Dress rehearsal for this ? On the contrary

parts.words: Dress rehearsal for this ? On the contrary
parts.note: a rehearsal of this act is really an undress rehearsal: the performer takes clothes off rather than putting them on

explanation.surface: A theatre company's dress rehearsal, with a cheeky aside that the show itself goes the other way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the contrary' flips 'Dress' to its opposite: the act being practised is one of undressing, slowly and to music.
explanation.definitionFit: A burlesque act in which a performer gradually removes clothing is the reverse of dressing up.

clue.text: Support at base of column, only round its head

indicators.note: round means the word for only goes around the letter

parts.note: sole means only, as in the sole survivor

indicators.note: its head means the first letter of the word column

explanation.surface: Description of a part supporting a pillar at its foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'its head' gives C, the first letter of 'column', which SOLE goes 'round'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain plinth or block forms the foot on which a column or statue stands.

clue.text: Taken with ale for a good time in Gibraltar?

definitions.text: Taken with ale for a good time in Gibraltar?

parts.words: Taken with ale for a good time in Gibraltar?
parts.note: 'cakes and ale' means a good time, and Gibraltar is known as the Rock

explanation.surface: Something to have with beer when out for fun in Gibraltar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cakes and ale' is an old phrase (from Twelfth Night) for merrymaking; Gibraltar is called the Rock, so its cakes would be these.
explanation.definitionFit: These small hard-crusted buns could jokingly be the baked goods of the Rock of Gibraltar.

clue.text: When women race in Olney before …

definitions.text: When women race in Olney before …

parts.words: When women race in Olney before …
parts.note: the town of Olney holds a famous race for women tossing pancakes on the day before Lent, which the next clue begins

explanation.surface: The date of a women's race in a Buckinghamshire town, the day before something.
explanation.walkthrough: Olney, a town in Buckinghamshire, England, holds a women's pancake race every Shrove Tuesday. The dots run on to the next clue, which starts with 'Lent'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrove Tuesday, the day before Lent begins, is when Olney runs its pancake race.

clue.text: … Lent — tie possible. Give it a name

indicators.note: possible suggests one possible arrangement of the letters, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A continuation: Lent might end in a draw; now name it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possible' rearranges LENT and TIE.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a book or other work a title is to name it.

clue.text: Work for newspaper in action about plot

indicators.note: about signals that the word for action goes around the word for plot

parts.note: a suit is a legal action
a bed is a garden plot

explanation.surface: A journalist's job in action on some plot or story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is only a link; a suit at law is an action, and a garden bed is a plot.
explanation.definitionFit: Checking and correcting copy before printing is a newspaper desk job.

clue.text: To exchange, hands back

indicators.note: back tells us the word for hands is read from right to left

parts.note: paws is a jocular word for hands

explanation.surface: A request to trade, with the hands passed back over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns PAWS round.
explanation.definitionFit: To trade one thing for another is to make a switch.

clue.text: Drew a sort of bird

indicators.note: a sort of means a reworked version of the letters, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone sketched a kind of bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges DREW A.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-legged shore bird that feeds in shallow water, like a heron or stilt.

clue.text: Such the career of a Savoyard slave of duty

definitions.text: Such the career of a Savoyard slave of duty

parts.words: Such the career of a Savoyard slave of duty
parts.note: in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Pirates of Penzance, subtitled The Slave of Duty, Frederic is apprenticed to buccaneers

explanation.surface: A description of the working life of a Gilbert and Sullivan character.
explanation.walkthrough: Gilbert and Sullivan operas are called Savoy operas; The Pirates of Penzance is subtitled The Slave of Duty, and its hero is apprenticed to a band of buccaneers.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes freebooters who rob at sea, the career of the operetta's hero.

clue.text: Wife's rebuke confounded Eric with cruel taunt

indicators.note: confounded means mixed up, so the letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A wife's scolding confused poor Eric with its harsh mockery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confounded' rearranges ERIC with CRUEL TAUNT.
explanation.definitionFit: An old phrase for a wife's scolding of her husband in bed, behind the bed curtains.

clue.text: Head milk supplier

definitions.meaning: slang for the human skull or noggin
the palm-tree nut holds a milky liquid inside its shell

explanation.definitionFit: Slang calls a person's skull a nut of this kind, and the tropical nut itself yields a milky juice.

clue.text: A pound is returned under error

indicators.note: is returned signals that the pound abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: lb is the abbreviation for a pound in weight
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone notes a pound coming back short, owing to a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is returned' turns LB (a pound weight) into BL, followed by UNDER as printed.
explanation.definitionFit: A clumsy mistake or gaffe is an error.

clue.text: " A savage place! as holy and" (Coleridge)

definitions.text: " A savage place! as holy and" (Coleridge)

parts.words: " A savage place! as holy and" (Coleridge)
parts.note: a quotation from Kubla Khan with its closing word left blank for the solver to supply

explanation.surface: A line from Coleridge's poem Kubla Khan, with the last word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: The full line in Kubla Khan is 'A savage place! as holy and enchanted / As e'er beneath a waning moon was haunted'. A clue like this tests whether you know the quotation.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem describes the chasm as bewitched, under a magic spell, holy and uncanny.

clue.text: Fortune teller's card causes sailor to return

parts.note: tar is an old word for a seaman

indicators.note: return tells us the little word 'to' is turned round

explanation.surface: A clairvoyant turns up a card that sends a seaman home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'causes' is only a link. A tar (from tarpaulin) is old slang for a sailor; the tiny word 'to' is the piece that turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: Fortune tellers lay out cards from this special pack for divination.

clue.text: A North American fraternity member is back in this joint

indicators.note: is back signals that the word for the fraternity member is read backwards

parts.note: the Elks are an American fraternal order, so a member is an Elk

explanation.surface: A northern American lodge member has trouble with a joint in his leg.
explanation.walkthrough: The Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks is a US social club, like the Freemasons; 'is back' turns the member round, and 'in this joint' points to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The joint linking foot and leg is a body hinge, so 'this joint' points to it.

clue.text: Egyptian dancing-girl winning at chess for the university

annotationWithheld.why: Egyptian dancing-girl winning at chess for the university: ALMA (dancing-girl) + MATE (winning at chess) gives ALMAMATE; no clue word supplies the final R
annotationWithheld.clue: Egyptian dancing-girl winning at chess for the university

clue.text: Not essential to insert 'eleven cents change

indicators.note: change tells us the letters are rearranged into a new order

parts.note: XI is eleven in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone thinks it unnecessary to put in eleven cents' worth of change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' looks like loose coins alongside the cents, but it is the anagram signal working on INSERT and XI; the C for cents is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Something coming from outside rather than being part of a thing's nature is inessential.

clue.text: Give up manoeuvring cars if on ice

indicators.note: manoeuvring suggests moving pieces about, so these letters are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Advice to stop driving cars about on icy roads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'manoeuvring' rearranges CARS IF to SACRIF; 'on' then sets ICE beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To surrender something valued for a greater good is to forgo it.

clue.text: The butcher being more so than other men ?

definitions.text: The butcher being more so than other men ?

parts.words: The butcher being more so than other men ?
parts.note: butcher is read as 'more butch', a man more manly and tough than other men

explanation.surface: A tradesman who carves meat being described as more of something than other men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butcher' looks like the meat trader but is read as the comparative of butch, meaning more manly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone more butch has more of the manly qualities expected of men.

clue.text: Drive round a quarter-a way to get jurymen

indicators.note: round signals that the word for drive goes around the other letters

parts.note: to impel is to drive forward
N is north, a compass quarter

explanation.surface: Instructions to drive round a district to round up a jury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' puts IMPEL around A and N (north, one of the four compass quarters).
explanation.definitionFit: To enrol people on a jury list is how a jury is assembled.

clue.text: Serious composer, Thomas, in the East of France

indicators.note: in signals that the composer goes inside the French word

parts.note: est is French for east
Thomas Arne was the English composer of Rule, Britannia!

explanation.surface: A grave English composer working in eastern France.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Arne (1710-78) wrote Rule, Britannia!; the clue uses French for 'the East', a common crossword trick when France is named.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sincere and solemn in intent is being serious.

clue.text: Sort of government, see, by the state

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning see or behold
Cal is the abbreviation for California, a US state

explanation.surface: A remark about forms of government being set by the state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' just puts the pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Town and county councils make up the regional tier of government, as opposed to national.

clue.text: Some complicated point for a lawgiver

indicators.note: complicated tells us the letters of the word beside it are jumbled

parts.note: S is south, a compass point

explanation.surface: A tricky legal point is put to a legislator.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complicated' rearranges SOME, then S (south, a compass point) is added.
explanation.definitionFit: The Biblical prophet brought the Ten Commandments down from Sinai and is called the great lawgiver of Israel.

clue.text: Remakes cigars I dropped — some neck !

indicators.note: remakes means the remaining letters are built again in a new order
dropped means the letter is taken out of the word

explanation.surface: Someone rolls cigars afresh and loses some, to an exclamation of cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropped' removes I from CIGARS, and 'Remakes' rearranges CGARS.
explanation.definitionFit: The scrawny neck end of a carcass of mutton or veal is a cheap cut.

clue.text: For Wesley all the world was such a district

definitions.text: For Wesley all the world was such a district

parts.words: For Wesley all the world was such a district
parts.note: John Wesley said 'I look upon all the world as my parish', so the world was a church district to him

explanation.surface: A remark about the founder of Methodism seeing the whole world as his patch.
explanation.walkthrough: John Wesley, the founder of Methodism, preached in the open air everywhere and famously said 'I look upon all the world as my parish'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes a church parish, the small district a minister serves.

clue.text: Vegetables in Jumblies vessel, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the word is judged by how it is said

parts.note: Edward Lear's Jumblies went to sea in a sieve, a vessel that lets water through

explanation.surface: Greens stowed aboard the Jumblies' boat.
explanation.walkthrough: In Edward Lear's poem The Jumblies, the Jumblies go to sea in a sieve, which of course lets water in.
explanation.definitionFit: These onion relatives are green vegetables, the Welsh emblem.

clue.text: Rare variety is tinned when ground

indicators.note: is, read with tinned, puts the jumbled letters inside the container

parts.note: a tinned thing is in a tin

indicators.note: variety suggests a different form of the word, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A rare type of produce is canned when it has been ground down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety' rearranges the letters of 'Rare' to ERRA, and 'is tinned' then means canned: placed within the container word. 'ground' looks like a verb but means land.
explanation.definitionFit: A stretch of land considered for its physical features is ground.

clue.text: Learned royalty has endlessly varied duties

parts.note: ER stands for Elizabeth Regina, the Queen

indicators.note: varied means the remaining letters are put in a new order
endlessly means the last letter of the next word is cut off

explanation.surface: A member of the royal family has a series of different engagements.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' removes the final S of 'duties' and 'varied' rearranges what is left; ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for the Queen, so royalty.
explanation.definitionFit: A deeply scholarly, well-read person is called this.

clue.text: Whither a girl almost returned after a beastly ride?

indicators.note: returned signals that the whole run is then read backwards
almost means the last letter of the word is left off

parts.note: girl loses its last letter; the four letters also sitting backwards across 'a girl' is a coincidence of this trimming, not a separate hidden run

explanation.surface: A question of where a young woman went, almost coming back after riding an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims GIRL to GIR; 'returned' turns A GIR round. The limerick's young lady of Riga rode on a tiger, and returned inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The limerick's young lady came from this Latvian capital, so it answers where she was heading.

clue.text: The joy of poetic skylarking

parts.note: Shelley's poem To a Skylark opens 'Hail to thee, blithe spirit', so the bird's poetic joy is its blithe quality

explanation.surface: A celebration of the happiness of poets fooling around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'skylarking' looks like horseplay, but points to Shelley's ode To a Skylark, which hails a 'blithe spirit'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being blithe means being carefree and cheerful, so the noun means gaiety or joy.
